articles.title: K-pop star Sunmi loves Notion and ear cleaning videos
articles.summary: Nearly 20 years into her music career Wonder Girls’ Sunmi is staying humble, but persistent.
articles.body: Sunmi is an undeniable force in K-pop. She first made her debut as a member of the Wonder Girls back in 2007, one of the first K-pop acts to really break through in the West. The English version of their single “Nobody” was the first K-pop song to hit the Billboard Hot 100 in October 2009. In 2010 Sunmi left the group to go back to school, but the siren call of a music career pulled her back in. She released her debut solo EP Full Moon in 2014. That began a run of award-winning releases for the pop star, including Song of the Year for “Gashina” at the Gaon Chart Music Awards. Despite her near-constant presence in the K-pop world as a solo artist and as a member of the Wonder Girls, whom she rejoined in 2015, Sumni only just released her first solo LP, Heart Maid, in 2025. This year she released the single “Forever July,” which blends ’90s R&B synths with rubbery bass and UK garage-inspired drums. Sunmi has called it one of her most personal songs. And she wasn’t afraid to get personal in our Q&A either, revealing details about her writing process, her greatest disappointment as an artist, and her love of ear cleaning videos. What is your most indispensable tool? My phone. I use the Notes app and Voice Memos a lot when I’m writing lyrics or making music. Whenever I have a good idea, I can immediately pull it out and write it down, so I really can’t live without it. Which is the most underappreciated? The Samsung Galaxy series. It has made my work environment so much easier. Team Galaxyyyyyy! What is the first app you install on a new phone or computer? These days, you can transfer all the apps and data from your previous device, so I don’t really have to install anything separately. But if that process didn’t exist, I’d probably install KakaoTalk, a messaging app, first. What is one thing you wish you could change about your phone? I have so many unnecessary photos and screenshots in my gallery. I wish there were a feature that could recognize similar or duplicate photos and group them together, so I could delete them all at once. What sites do you have pinned to your tab bar? Notion. I use it a lot because I work on many group projects. It’s convenient, but it takes quite a long time to get used to. I think the UI could use some improvement. How many tabs do you have open right now? Four: Notion, Google Drive, YouTube, and Claude. Which social media platform do you use the most? I don’t really use social media that much, but I think I use Instagram and X the most. What is your happy place online? Videos of people getting their ears cleaned on YouTube. What is your favorite gadget you’ve ever owned? I’m not really good with technology, but I think the Samsung Z Fold 8 that I’m using right now is probably my favorite device. I often need to work on documents or edit videos while I’m on the go, and it’s incredibly convenient. I can work with both hands on a wide screen, and it’s surprisingly light. It’s exactly the kind of device I’ve always needed. What game do you have the fondest memories of? MapleStory by Nexon. I played it when I was in elementary school, and even after becoming an adult, I would sometimes play the mobile version. The graphics really bring back memories of my childhood. Which tech trend do you wish would go away? Deepfakes. Ew. What is one thing you wish you had created? Stranger Things 5 and Game of Thrones 8. What creation are you most proud of? “Tail.” It’s a song that still gets me excited every time I perform it live. When I hold my breath, the audience holds their breath too, and when I explode, they explode with me. It creates this really unique experience. Which are you least proud of? “You Can’t Sit with Us.” It was the first song where I ever tried rapping. But the lyrics and even my voice were terrible. What’s the best piece of advice you’ve ever received? Always stay humble. You should never let yourself become arrogant. What is your current obsession? I really love ice cream. Korean summers are shockingly hot, so it’s hard to survive without ice cream. I absolutely love Salt & Straw’s Salted Caramel Waffle Cone, but there’s nothing quite like it in Korea. What do you do when you need to focus? I find a small space to organize my thoughts. What do you do when you’re feeling stuck? I say “No?” out loud. For example, if I start thinking to myself, “I can’t do this,” I immediately say “No?” out loud. When was the last time you went somewhere without your phone? When I’m shooting, I leave my phone with my manager. Even during short breaks, I barely look at my phone. But I’ve never actually gone somewhere without my phone. What’s the last piece of physical media you bought? The Senses of an Everydayist, a new essay collection by lyricist Kim Eana. She sent me a copy as a gift when it was published, but I believe there’s something meaningful about personally buying and reading someone’s creative work, so I bought a copy online. articles.title: Sydney Sweeney y Marilyn Monroe comparten un inesperado vínculo familiar: ¡primas novenas en una generación!
articles.standfirst: Lo descubre una investigación genealógica y viene de la rama del padre
articles.summary: Lo descubre una investigación genealógica y viene de la rama del padre
articles.body: Sorpresas que da la vida. A veces se dice que la vida es un pañuelo, pues se ha encontrado un vínculo especialmente llamativo. Sydney Sweeney y Marilyn Monroe tienen más cosas en común de las que muchos imaginaban. Más allá de las constantes comparaciones por su imagen y su proyección en Hollywood, una investigación ha encontrado un sorprendente nexo entre ambas actrices: ¡comparten raíces familiares! Los genes... El hallazgo ha sido realizado por MyHeritage, una plataforma especializada en genealogía, que ha concluido que la estrella de Euphoria y el gran icono del cine estadounidense coinciden en la misma línea familiar por parte de padre. Es más, dicha empresa ha hecho un estudio que las sitúa como primas novenas con una generación de diferencia. Roi Mandel, que es el director de investigación de la compañía, explicó que el estudio nació por las continuas comparaciones entre ambas figuras de Hollywood. "La gente siempre ha establecido paralelismos entre Sydney Sweeney y Marilyn Monroe, pero comprobar que existía una conexión real en su árbol genealógico nos llevó a profundizar en los archivos", explicaba. Según dicho estudio efectuado, el vínculo entre ambas mujeres se remonta varios siglos atrás. Los investigadores identificaron a Ezra Perry, un colono inglés que vivió entre 1625 y 1689 y se estableció en Massachusetts, como el antepasado común de las dos intérpretes. Por todo ello, la investigación sostiene que Steven Sweeney, padre de Sydney Sweeney, y Charles Stanley Gifford, padre de Marilyn Monroe, descienden directamente de Perry. Esta conexión convierte a ambas actrices en primas novenas, aunque con una generación de diferencia. La coincidencia resulta todavía más llamativa porque Sweeney nunca ha ocultado su admiración por Monroe. La actriz estadounidense ha hecho referencia en varias ocasiones a la leyenda de Hollywood y a la influencia que ha tenido en la cultura popular. En los Governors Awards de 2025, Sweeney llamó la atención al aparecer con un peinado inspirado en Los caballeros las prefieren rubias, una de las películas más emblemáticas de Marilyn Monroe. Ahora, gracias a esta investigación, aquel parecido que muchos seguidores señalaban desde hace tiempo no se limita a la imagen o al éxito en la gran pantalla, sino que también tiene una explicación que se remonta más de tres siglos atrás.

articles.title: When Nana Patekar revealed he didn't have money to pay for his father's treatment so he died in the hospital: 'That hesitation stays with you'
articles.summary: Veteran actor Nana Patekar, who passed away on Thursday, October 8, leaves behind a remarkable body of work and a legacy that extends beyond his
articles.body: Veteran actor Nana Patekar, who passed away on Thursday, October 8, leaves behind a remarkable body of work and a legacy that extends beyond his performances on screen. Over the years, the actor has also offered glimpses into the personal experiences that shaped him. One such moment was when he opened up about the painful loss of his father, whom he could not afford to get treated.Reflecting on his early struggles, Nana spoke about how his financial situation gradually improved after he entered the film industry. However, by the time he began earning well, it was too late to save his father, who passed away in a hospital when the family could not afford his treatment."I started earning money from films. Initially, I earned a little, and then I started earning a lot. But when my father was ill, I didn't have the money to pay for his treatment, and he died in the hospital," he recalled in an interview with NDTV in 2024.The actor also revisited the difficult nights he spent outside the hospital with a friend while his father was admitted. Unable to stay inside overnight, the two would sit on the stairs or the footpath, playing Antakshari as they waited anxiously for news about his father's condition."We used to sit on the stairs or on the footpath outside the hospital. We weren't allowed to stay inside overnight, so we would sit outside and play Antakshari. My friend was there with me. You never knew when someone would come out and tell you that your father was no more," Nana said.Looking back, the actor expressed the regret of not having enough money to secure better medical care for his father. Despite achieving considerable success in his career, the memory of being unable to help his father during his final days continued to affect him emotionally."If I had had the money, I could have got him better medicines and taken him to a better hospital. articles.title: Traditional dolls set to catch eyeballs at Navaratri Bombe Habba
articles.summary: Chikkamagaluru Navaratri Bombe Habba starts Oct 11 at Ranganna Kalyana Mantapa, showcasing traditional doll displays; entry free for 9 days.
articles.body: Chikkamagaluru: For nine days, stories of gods, kings, glimpses of village life and contemporary society will come alive in miniature form, not on a stage but on tiers through beautifully arranged dolls. This is the unique charm of Bombe Habba.To preserve the rich traditions, art and history associated with Navaratri, the Chikkamagaluru District Brahmin Mahasabha will organise a nine-day Navaratri Bombe Habba at Ranganna Kalyana Mantapa from Oct 11. District president P Manjunatha Joshi described the event as more than just an exhibition. “It is a living museum of our culture and heritage,” he told reporters on Friday.According to Joshi, the tradition of displaying dolls during Navaratri occupies a special place in Karnataka’s cultural heritage. “Kings and maharajas used to install and worship Pattada Bombe, or royal dolls, in their palaces. What began as a royal custom gradually spread to ordinary households during the reign of the Mysore rulers,” he said.A practice once confined to palaces has now become an integral part of celebrations in homes across the region.Last year, seven renowned Bombe Manes -Anjanadri, Andal, Doopadakol, Mysuru, Myurashilpi, Kanaka Shankaregowda and Jaji - showcased their collections at the venue. Organisers expect even greater participation this year, with more families displaying treasured heirloom dolls passed down through generations.A Bombe Mane is much more than a collection of dolls. Each tier narrates a distinct story.The lower steps typically depict scenes from everyday life, including markets, villages, weddings and farming activities. The middle tiers feature themes such as Ashtalakshmi, social messages and contemporary issues, while the topmost levels showcase deities, scenes from the Puranas and the Pattada Bombe, symbolising royal authority and prosperity.“The exhibition will feature displays on the worship of deities, stories from the puranas, social and artistic themes, the significance of Pattada Bombe, village life and contemporary issues,” Joshi said. The highlight of this year’s exhibition will be a pair of intricately carved sandalwood dolls representing a king and queen, he added.Entry to the exhibition is free. articles.title: DistroKid has been quietly taking down songs in response to UMG lawsuit
articles.summary: Artists are frustrated with the lack of transparency around DistroKid taking down their songs in response to the UMG lawsuit.
articles.body: Artists are taking to social media to complain that DistroKid has unceremoniously removed their work without notice. Now DistroKid has confirmed to The Verge that the takedowns are a direct response to claims made by UMG. The label filed a lawsuit in September claiming that DistroKid has created an “AI-slop pipeline.” Artists are saying that their non-AI works are being caught up in the purge, however. Musician and self-described “Video Game boy” McGwire reported that six of his songs had been removed from streaming. As has been the case with others, McGwire says that there was no communication from DistroKid before or after the removals, and that he had to contact the company for an explanation. DistroKid also makes it exceedingly difficult to contact them. McGwire first had to have a “lengthy circular conversation” with a bot before getting hold of a live agent. One of the songs removed was a cover of Stevie Wonder’s “Isn’t She Lovely,” which he claims to have had a proper license for. Another track used a beat he purchased through a marketplace, which others had also licensed. Most infuriating for McGwire was a song removed for an uncleared sample. The song he allegedly sampled was released two years after his track. Music producer and marketing pro Jesse Cannon told The Verge that, “DistroKid gave up on customer service about two years ago.” He was sympathetic to artists’ plight, but seemed unsurprised by the company’s indifference. “They should have allowed artists to have recourse in this and a warning to debate,” he said, “but I’ve been told by former employees they see customer service as a waste of profits since they have such a high market share and remain ubiquitous.” Much of the frustration from artists stems from the lack of communication and recourse. Nerdcore rapper Insane Ian posted that he “had an original song taken down with no warning, and they wouldn’t tell me why either.” Rapper King Chase also struggled to get through to a person at DistroKid. He told The Verge that an entire album for an artist he had been working with was removed with no communication or explanation. “The album had been up for 3-4 years without incident,” he said, and that there had been “no copyright strikes or anything either.” Amanda Ferri, DistroKid’s VP of Artist Services, told The Verge that “A very small number of recordings distributed through DistroKid have been removed in response to claims made by UMG. We strongly dispute the allegations underlying UMG’s lawsuit and regret the disruption to affected artists. We are working to minimize that disruption while protecting artists’ ability to release their music.” Update October 10th, 2026: Added comment from Jesse Cannon.

articles.body: Amitabh Bachchan turns 84 today, October 11, and as wishes pour in from family, friends and fans across the world, it is a good time to revisit a heartfelt conversation with his son, Abhishek Bachchan. While Abhishek has always looked up to his father as his hero, he has also spoken about the man behind the legendary star and how, at the end of the day, Amitabh is a father and grandfather like any other.In an exclusive interview with ETimes last year, Abhishek reflected on his 26-year journey in the film industry, including its highs and lows. When asked whether his father felt proud of the work he had done since his debut, Abhishek spoke about how parents, Amitabh Bachchan and Jaya Bachchan value their children's efforts beyond professional success."I think my father and mother would be proud of anything that I do, provided they know that I've given it my best. People forget he's also a father. For us, Amitabh Bachchan is a hero. So, we never look at it from that lens, but he's also a family man! He's a father, he's a grandfather. For some reason we think, 'Oh no, he's not allowed to be that or be human', but he is. He's also a father, and my mother is also a mother. I'm their child. They're allowed to feel the way every other parent would feel."Abhishek also spoke about how growing up in a family constantly associated with fame helped him maintain perspective on success and popularity. Explaining why he has never been overly attached to the idea of fame, he said that his experiences at home taught him how quickly public attention can change."Fame is transient. I grew up with examples at home. When my father came home, he wasn't Amitabh Bachchan, he was my father. Fame aayega, jayega and you realise it with just a couple of films."Amitabh Bachchan is currently hosting the latest season of 'Kaun Banega Crorepati'. articles.title: In 2020, Steve McQueen’s son sold the actor’s former Malibu beach house for $7.2 million; two months later new owners paid $8.35 million, renovated the 4,335-square-foot retreat and listed it for $16.995 million
articles.summary: A former Malibu beach house belonging to Hollywood actor Steve McQueen returned to the luxury property market in 2022 after changing hands twice in 2020
articles.body: A former Malibu beach house belonging to Hollywood actor Steve McQueen returned to the luxury property market in 2022 after changing hands twice in 2020 and undergoing extensive renovations. According to the Coldwell Banker Realty listing, the 4,335-square-foot residence sits within the gated Victoria Point community in Malibu, California, and features oceanfront decks, expansive Pacific views and private beach access. The house was listed for $16.995 million after songwriter Ammar Malik and his wife, Chyna Bardarson, purchased it for $8.35 million, according to Architectural Digest.From Steve McQueen’s private retreat to a property saleSteve McQueen, known for films including Bullitt and The Great Escape, lived in the Malibu house with his then-wife, actor Ali MacGraw, during the 1970s. The property offered a quieter setting away from Hollywood, with access to the beach and views of the Pacific Ocean. McQueen, often nicknamed the “King of Cool”, was known for seeking privacy away from the entertainment industry. Marc Eliot’s 2012 biography describes how McQueen and MacGraw enjoyed walks along the beach near their home, where they could spend time away from public attention.The house later remained associated with McQueen’s legacy through its location and distinctive coastal setting. Its history also became a selling point when it returned to the real estate market decades after the actor’s death in 1980.A $7.2 million sale in 2020In July 2020, McQueen’s son, Chad McQueen, sold the Malibu property for $7.2 million, according to Architectural Digest. The sale marked a new chapter for the house, which had been connected to the actor’s private life for decades. Two months later, in September 2020, Malik and Bardarson bought the residence for $8.35 million. Malik, a songwriter known for co-writing popular tracks including Maroon 5’s “Moves Like Jagger”, later renovated the property. The two transactions showed a $1.15 million difference between the reported sale prices.Renovations and a $16.995 million asking priceAfter purchasing the property, Malik and Bardarson undertook extensive renovations. Malik told Inman that the couple spent well into seven figures renovating the property, including upgrading the plumbing and electrical systems. The renovated residence retained its emphasis on indoor-outdoor living. According to the Coldwell Banker Realty listing, the house has four bedrooms and five bathrooms, with large glass walls that open onto oceanfront decks. Its design connects the kitchen, dining and living areas with outdoor spaces overlooking the Pacific.The property also includes two primary suites, fireplaces, spa-style bathrooms, a three-car garage and a private staircase leading down to the beach. Its position within the gated Victoria Point community offers privacy, while its views extend along the coastline from Broad Beach towards Point Dume. In November 2022, the owners put the house on the market for $16.995 million. The asking price was more than double the $8.35 million they had paid in 2020, although a listing price does not establish the eventual selling price. The property was relisted for $14.995 million in June 2023 and sold for $13.6 million in September 2023, according to Coldwell Banker Realty’s property record.A Malibu home with Hollywood historyThe actor’s former home was presented to prospective buyers as a renovated beachside retreat rather than simply a celebrity-owned property. Its history with McQueen and MacGraw adds another dimension to the listing, recalling a period when the actor sought a quieter life outside Hollywood. The extensive renovations updated the house’s infrastructure and amenities, while its ocean-facing layout remained a central feature.The 2022 listing illustrates how a property’s value can be shaped by several factors, including location, improvements and historical associations. For McQueen’s former Malibu home, the combination of a private beach staircase, expansive decks, Pacific views and a connection to one of Hollywood’s best-known actors helped position it in the luxury real estate market.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: What happened before Ella Langley's Tulsa show was canceled
articles.summary: The 'Choosin' Texas' hitmaker's Tulsa tour stop was canceled Friday night after an alleged threat of 'great harm' involving gunfire and bombs.
articles.body:
Danica Livingston already had her nails done with butterflies and a dandelion, and her mom, Rita Livingston, was finishing up her makeup in their downtown Tulsa hotel room when they got the bad news that their long-awaited concert plans were canceled .

Ella Langley's highly anticipated show set for Friday, Oct. 9, at Tulsa's BOK Center was called off just hours before it was scheduled to start due to "a serious security threat involving the safety of fans, venue personnel, and the artist."

"Danica's birthday is in August, so she's been waiting two months for this," said Rita Livingston, of Duncan. "I was like, 'How do I look at this little girl and tell her that we're not going to get to do this?' ... She took it like an absolute champ. She looked at us and said, 'Well, better safe than sorry, and at least we're still together. We'll figure it out.' And that's what we did."

Rita and Danica Livingston — along with Melissa Kerr, of Tuttle, their sister-in-law and aunt, respectively — were among the about 19,000 fans left disappointed when the up-and-coming country music superstar's sold-out Tulsa show was abruptly canceled.

In identical graphics, both Langley and the venue announced the sudden cancellation on social media at about 4:45 p.m. Friday.

"The safety and well-being of everyone involved is our absolute priority, and after careful consideration, we have determined that the show cannot proceed," the social media message to ticketholders read in part. "We appreciate your understanding and cooperation as we prioritize the safety of all involved."

In a caption on her post, the record-setting "Choosin' Texas" hitmaker called canceling the concert an "incredibly difficult decision."

"This decision was made under the advisement of local authorities, the venue, and my security team," Langley added. "I know how much time, travel, money, and planning goes into coming to a show, and I can't tell you how sorry I am. This is not a decision that was made lightly. I was so looking forward to spending tonight with you, but your safety will always mean more to me than anything else. I refuse to put anyone in harm's way."

According to the "Important Show Update" announcing the cancelation, additional information and details regarding ticket refunds are to be shared as soon as possible. But Kerr, who bought the tickets to Langley's Tulsa concert as a 12th birthday present for her niece, told The Oklahoman on Saturday, Oct. 10, that she's already received her refund.

"So, I don't think they plan on rescheduling it," she said.

Neither representatives for Langley nor the BOK Center responded Saturday to The Oklahoman's requests for more information on the Tulsa concert cancelation .

Langley's blockbuster "The Dandelion Tour" is still scheduled to continue with a Saturday, Oct. 10, concert at United Supermarkets Arena in Lubbock, Texas. The second leg of the tour is set to conclude Oct. 31 at Grand Casino Arena in Saint Paul, Minnesota.

Ella Langley draws crowd to OKC Zoo Amphitheatre: Photos

Ella Langley's Tulsa concert canceled after alleged call threatening 'great harm' with gunfire and bombs

In a since-deleted post on the Tulsa Police Department's Facebook, Capt. Richard Meulenberg said in a video that officers conducted security sweeps of the BOK Center, including searches with bomb-sniffing dogs, as is routine for events at the downtown Tulsa venue.

Although the initial searches found no threats, he said police returned to the BOK Center after a call came in "saying that someone was going to (do) great harm to the people here at this event in the way of shots fired and bombs," according to a transcript of the video shared by the Saving Country Music blog.

"So we came out again in an overabundance of caution, used our bomb dogs again, searched the entire area, we could not find a credible threat here at the BOK Center," Meulenberg said in the since-deleted video. "We advised the group that was supposed to be performing tonight that we could not find a credible threat. We would never tell anybody if we couldn't find a credible threat to cancel their event. So they made the decision to cancel their event."

According to screenshots of the now-deleted post , the Tulsa Police Department said the incident is under investigation and that "it is unfortunate that some nefarious characters successfully disrupted the event, ruining the evening for thousands of people."

Neither Meulenberg nor any member of the Tulsa Police Communications Unit responded to The Oklahoman's emailed request for more information.

Disappointed Oklahoma fans believe 'better safe than sorry' when it comes to the concert cancelation

Although she had mixed feelings after hearing the Tulsa Police statements, Rita Livingston said she thinks organizers made the best decision in canceling the concert.

"That's my 12-year-old daughter, and I would rather be safe than sorry. I don't want to put her in harm's way," Livingston said as they made the three-hour drive back to southern Oklahoma on Saturday. "Melissa and I spent probably two hours trying to figure out how we could get to Lubbock, and if we could afford tickets and a hotel room, and ... we just finally were like, 'We can't justify that,' because the ticket prices were going up."

So, the trio spent their Friday night in their Tulsa hotel room, eating sushi, drinking dirty sodas and watching "The Golden Girls" before heading home. They will make other plans for her daughter's belated 12th birthday, she said.

"Whether it's prank calling or genuinely serious, unfortunately, we live in a time where you just don't know anymore. ... After what happened in Las Vegas to Jason Aldean , it's like 'OK, well, I don't want anything happening to my family, so I understand.' And you're grateful for that, even though you're disappointed in the moment," Livingston said, referring to the deadly 2017 mass shooting at the Route 91 Harvest Music Festival.

Likewise, Oklahoma singer-songwriter Mallory Eagle spent her night eating tacos and experiencing a kind of "weird fever dream" instead of playing a free outdoor Tulsa show in conjunction with Langley's concert. Eagle and her band had just finished soundcheck for her latest performance in the BOK Center's "Rock the Block" outdoor pre-concert street party series when she got a call that her show had been canceled along with Langley's.

"I got a call from my point of contact, who said, 'Hey, you guys need to pack up and go. We have a security threat, and the show's canceled,' which was a bit jarring to the system. You think you're gonna be getting on stage and having this thing you've really looked forward ... but everyone's safety is more important," Eagle said. "What was scariest is that it just was vague. We weren't told any specifics. We were just told 'it's a security threat.' So, the mind can really wander at that point."

Although the cancelation was announced more than an hour before doors were scheduled to open at 6 p.m. for Langley's show, Eagle said there were already fans lining up outside the arena when word got out that the concert had been scrapped.

"My friend and I went to dinner after ... and there were all these little Ella Langley fans, these girls in their little cowboy boots and T-shirts that say 'Ella.' And we're all just kind of having a sad dinner," she said. "But it was also (with) gratitude; they did what they thought best."

The BOK Center is scheduled to host its next concert at 7 p.m. Saturday, Oct. 10, when beloved gospel singer CeCe Winans performs .

articles.title: 'Happy Days' star Anson Williams says he had to create a second career because sitcom pay wasn't enough
articles.summary: Anson Williams reveals how conversations with David Cassidy and Barry Williams inspired him to pitch a musical act on the iconic sitcom.
articles.body: When playing Potsie Weber on "Happy Days" didn't pay well enough, actor Anson Williams came up with a side hustle: a music career. In a recent interview on the "Still Here Hollywood Podcast," the 77-year-old actor revealed the singing sideline was simply a matter of 1970s economics. "On 'Happy Days' we didn't have the same salaries they have today. Not even close," he said. "Nine hundred dollars an episode, $1,200 an episode. It was fine back then, but...it's not a lifetime of earnings there." Williams said that after speaking to "Partridge Family" star David Cassidy and Barry Williams, of "The Brady Bunch," about how much money they were making by taking their singing acts off the show, he thought to himself, "Wait a minute. I sing. If I can convince Garry to put a band on the show, maybe I can get booked, and maybe I can get some extra income." ‘BRADY BUNCH’ CAST MADE NEARLY NOTHING FROM DECADES OF RERUNS, EVE PLUMB CLAIMS After speaking with the show's creator, Garry Marshall, about the possibility of putting together a band to perform at Arnold's, the burger joint where Fonzie held court, the legendary director gave him a chance. Marshall told him he would have to pick a song and sing it to a bulldog, telling him, "If you're good, I get laughs. If you're bad, I get laughs. You're going to sing the bulldog." "So I do it and then the letters start coming in, and he goes 'The people like it. The people like it.' He goes, 'We'll do more. You're in charge of it though,'" Williams recalled. "Then I got a major agent for that and started getting booked at state fairs for 10 years." Williams added that his idea to sing on the show "started this whole career" that ended up being better for him monetarily, and was "just a whole other life experience." After finding success as a musician as well as an actor, Williams said that Marshall approached him to express how proud he was of the actor, telling him, "You found an opportunity, and you're helping the show." "And Garry Marshall and Jerry Paris, our director, thought, ‘What if we changed the whole tone? What if we make it a live audience sitcom?’" Williams recalled. "So, half the season, one camera. articles.title: Blackpink’s Lisa Manobal: How the K-pop star faced a race scandal
articles.summary: Film-maker Sue Kim talks about having unprecedented access to K-Pop idol Lisa Manobal at her most candid.
articles.body:
What's it like to be the main character of an online scandal?

That's one of the questions raised in a new documentary about Lisa Manobal – one quarter of K-pop phenomenon Blackpink and a breakout star of TV show The White Lotus.

The film captures an unfolding controversy, as leaked videos show Blackpink using racial slurs when they were teenage trainees in the K-pop system.

The clips, which emerged last year, showed the band covering US rap songs during rehearsals. Explicit language, including the n-word, was left uncensored.

The scandal blew up while Lisa was rehearsing for a pivotal performance at the Coachella Festival in 2025.

Offended and upset, some fans demanded an apology - but the band's record label, forbade the members from issuing a statement.

With Lisa's team in crisis mode, documentarian Sue Kim followed Lisa into her dressing room.

"I said, 'Look, I know this is new. I know you guys are wildly confused and hurt, but this is your time to say whatever you want to say - even if you're just processing your thoughts and telling us what you're feeling," Kim tells the BBC.

The film-maker "honestly expected her to say no".

Instead, Lisa lay down on a sofa and spoke from the heart.

"It's bad," the singer says in the documentary, with a mixture of shame and nerves.

Lisa explains she was "15 or 16" when the videos were shot and "didn't know that [word] was sensitive because I'm from Thailand and my first language is not English".

Having only heard the term in rap music, she was unaware of its offensive history.

"Now I would never ever do that because, now, I've got education," she says. "Now I know better.

It is a vulnerable and human response - and nothing like the scripted PR apology you might expect. (Lisa has since apologised publicly in an interview with Variety, although some people remained unconvinced ).

Kim says Lisa’s in-the-moment reaction is "one of the most important scenes" in her documentary, Always Lalisa, which hits cinemas on Monday, 12 October.

"There was no premeditation on Lisa's part, there was no media training," she adds.

"I asked her one question and she just talked for an hour, and everything came out, and it's all stream of consciousness.

"And what you see with Lisa in that moment is so genuine, it's impossible not to feel compassion for her."

The incident overshadowed what was supposed to be a triumphant launch for Lisa's debut solo album, Alter Ego.

In the film, the singer receives death threats, but presses ahead with public appearances while safety concerns are "spinning in my head".

"To a certain extent I have to take [criticism] and compromise," she says, exhausted, "but sometimes, it's too much".

In a world of sanitised celebrity profiles, Kim's portrayal of upheaval and discomfort is unusual. She asks Lisa about bad reviews, and captures the star being scolded by her vocal coach for lack of effort.

That said, the documentary was commissioned by the film division of the star's record label (which also made the recent, and much less revealing, Oasis documentary ), so it is still ultimately a marketing product.

Even the most abrasive moments are calibrated to present Lisa in a good light - but the director credits the star with ensuring the film was not a mere puff piece.

"You never know when you meet an artist how transparent they'll be. And I have to give all credit to Lisa because she allowed us almost total access," Kim says.

"And when I showed her the film, she never asked me to remove a single scene. That's exceptional."

The film's main storyline is about Lisa taking a break from K-pop to pursue crossover success in the Western music market.

When we meet her, she is one of the world's most famous women, with millions of record sales and brand deals with Louis Vuitton and Bvlgari.

But she is trapped by a K-pop system that forbids her from drinking alcohol and having adult relationships.

"I don't want my dating to be the thing to hurt Blackpink's popularity," she says in the film. "But when I turned 25, I realised that this is not how you're supposed to live your life."

As a result, Lisa makes an early decision to cut ties with Korean entertainment company YG, who discovered her as a teenager, and signs a new deal with RCA Records in the US.

"Knowing her as I do, that took an immense amount of courage," says Kim.

"In general, she is a very kind, sweet person - and sometimes personalities like that, they don't want to rock the boat.

"Having been trained in the K-pop system from an early age, she grew acclimatised to obedience. Declaring that she wants a break is such a disruption to that way of life that I can only imagine it must have been building inside her for years."

The potential rewards for going solo were phenomenal – but so were the risks.

In the film, we see Lisa struggling to assert herself in the recording studio, and tearfully battling nerves over her singing voice.

At the age of 25, she is still curiously child-like. The fierce independence of her solo single New Woman sounds more like aspiration than fact.

Kim says that began to change as they filmed.

"I saw a person who was very tentative and unsure of herself slowly starting to unfold her wings. Making mistakes, but also getting back up on the horse."

Kim locates an inner confidence in early home videos of Lisa competing in talent shows, drawing parallels between that precocious seven-year-old and the young woman who is gradually reclaiming her agency.

She doggedly pursues a role in the third season of hit TV drama The White Lotus, self-taping an audition that wins her the role of kind-hearted wellness coach Mook Sornsin.

On set, she shrugs off the restrictive moral code of her pop career.

"Lisa threw more parties than anyone else," notes the show's executive producer in an interview.

"And the defining characteristic of a Lisa party is tequila shots."

Kim did not partake in the hedonism. In fact, the film-maker and her crew were regularly falling sick as they tried to keep up with Lisa's ridiculous schedule.

"But when we premiered the film in Toronto, Lisa found me and she brought bottles of tequila, and that was like the perfect christening of the film," she laughs.

The movie ends in June 2025 as Lisa returns to Seoul and rejoins Blackpink. As she unpacks her bags, she is clearly conflicted.

"It's bittersweet, and I think that's OK," says Kim.

"I don't think people should take it as like, 'Oh, she hates Blackpink'. It's more that she was reflecting on this year of freedom and worrying that she wouldn't be able to retain that. And that's a very astute fear to have."

In the year since, Lisa has already wrapped up her Blackpink duties and started phase two of her solo career with the single Sawadika. Kim says she is not surprised.

"Spending the year away from the K-pop system in the US really opened her horizons," the director says.

"She was exposed to a different kind of entertainment system where they're not held to a vow of chastity. If two star performers link up, it's almost like they get more power.

"That gave her a sense of like, 'Oh, I could have a different life. I might not lose my career if I want to get married and have children'.

"So I think part of the reason why Lisa's interested in continuing her solo career is that it might give her a little bit more personal freedom to be who she is."
